text.p: America Online Inc. said Thursday that membership in the world's largest online service has surpassed 8 million as its unlimited pricing plan attracted a record number of subscribers.

But the Dulles, Va.-based company has experienced growing pains in the United States in the form of service outages -- including a partial outage of nearly four hours Wednesday -- and subscribers frustrated because efforts to dial in have encountered repeated busy signals.
America Online, or AOL, said local services launched in Britain, Canada, Germany and France had grown to more than half a million in 14 months.

Wall Street was astounded by the faster-than-expected growth in U.S. membership, fuelling a $3.375 jump in AOL's stock to $41.50, most of it at the end of the day, said Abhishek Gami, an analyst at Nesbitt Burns Securities in Chicago.
In the quarter ended in December, AOL added 1.2 million subscribers, including 500,000 in December alone, its biggest month ever, the company said.

AOL, which was hit this week by three class-action lawsuits, tried to address problems brought on by the surge in membership by saying it will increase its investment in expanding its network system to $350 million from $250 million.

The company also said it will sharply reduce marketing activities in this quarter as it continues to meet the needs of current members. For the time being, AOL will stop airing a nationwide television advertising campaign featuring the theme song from "The Jetsons" cartoon.
The company said it will sharply reduce the number of mailings of free trial disks, especially to cities where its customers are experiencing the most busy signals.
AOL said that between now and June it plans to increase by 75 percent the current total of 200,000-plus modems in its AOLNet system. More modems will allow more customers to dial in at the same time.

AOL will also break ground next month on a 180,000-square-foot data centre. The company said it plans to seek other ways to increase capacity and is promoting and supporting alternate ways to get AOL through work or schools.
AOL said it will add 600 additional customer support people over the next six months, bringing the total to 4,500.

Since AOL first switched its members to unlimited access for a flat rate of $19.95 a month on Dec. 1, it has been inundated with subscribers, some of whom stay on the service all day, making it difficult for users to sign on during peak hours, such as evenings and weekends.

In the past four days, mounting subscriber anger has led to three class-ction lawsuits filed against the company, with allegations ranging from breach of contract for failure to provide services to false advertising.
Attorneys general in several states have confirmed they are in talks with AOL to seek some remedy to the growing consumer complaints.
Analyst Gami said he was not concerned about the lawsuits or the inquiries by the attorneys general and said AOL is doing everything it can to meet customer demand.

To add to AOL's problems, late Wednesday afternoon, it had to shut down half its system when it noticed around 3 p.m. EST that more people could not sign on. The system ran at 50 percent capacity until 7:30 p.m. EST and full capacity was not reached until 8 p.m.

AOL officials said Wednesday's partial outage was not caused by the massive demand for its service. They said it took a few hours to find the problem because it had just conducted its bimonthly system shutdown Tuesday night and there were more procedures to review in order to find the problem.
The problem turned out to be a glitch in a piece of hardware that directs the flow of data in a network.

Gami said things like outage "results in a lot of bad press ... but when you have days like this, despite all the nasty things people are saying about them, they are growing at least double the rate of their competitors."

In his monthly letter to members, AOL Chairman Steve Case addressed the problems, saying "We all dial in from our homes at night, just like you do, so we see the problems firsthand. And we're working day and night to fix them."

AOL said the current usage of its network is exceeding its most aggressive forecasts, much of it due to the unlimited pricing plan. In December, its usage skyrocketed to more than 100 million hours, up from 60 million hours in November.
